body: probably the more correct solution here is to avoid pytest's specialized assert formatting when it detects that `__eq__` is overridden (since it's not going to accurately represent the underlying equality comparins)

it might also not be a bad idea for pytest to check if its numpy and use the numpy equals there as we do check numpy in a number of places - im under the impression a lot of the numpy handling should get a own plugin module by now
@RonnyPfannschmidt that would create a bug in the other direction in the default case (since `dataclass` is just going to use `==` and if we used numpy's comparison then it would be different)

> probably the more correct solution here is to avoid pytest's specialized assert formatting when it detects that `__eq__` is overridden (since it's not going to accurately represent the underlying equality comparins)

This seems like the most robust solution.

body: @RonnyPfannschmidt  I can try to work on this one if anyone haven't yet

Any tip on how we can determine if the `__eq__` method is overridden?
I've tried using `__code__` attribute but I don't think this is the right direction
off hand, i'm not sure, - @hynek from attrs may have a hint

it seems to be a little tricky since the method is generated -- one way would maybe be to compare the `co_filename` of `__eq__.__code__` (which appears to be `<string>` when it's overridden, or whatever the module filename is otherwise)
I remember that @willmcgugan did similar work for rich about detecting if repr was overwritten, so maybe he can help.

@hynek Thanks!
I think I found it: https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich/blob/07d51ffc1aee6f16bd2e5a25b4e82850fb9ed778/rich/pretty.py#L68

When I look deeper into the problem, I see it comes in many forms, consider the following code:
```python
import numpy as np
import attr

@attr.s
class SimpleDataObject:
    a = attr.ib(eq=attr.cmp_using(eq=np.array_equal))


left = SimpleDataObject(np.array([1, 2]))
right = SimpleDataObject(np.array([2, 1]))
assert right == left
```
Running this code under a test will also produce the same problem mentioned in the issue:
```
        left = SimpleDataObject(np.array([1, 2]))
        right = SimpleDataObject(np.array([2, 1]))
>       assert right == left
E       assert SimpleDataObject(a=array([2, 1])) == SimpleDataObject(a=array([1, 2]))
E         (pytest_assertion plugin: representation of details failed: c:\users\yuvals\pytest\src\_pytest\assertion\util.py:457: ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous. Use a.any() or a.all().
E          Probably an object has a faulty __repr__.)
```
Apart from checking if the `dataclass` or the `attrs.define` decorated class  (`attr.s` seems to ignore the customdefined `__eq__`) has a custom `__eq__` method, should we also consider handling attributes which raise an exception during there comparison, something like:
```python
>       assert right == left
E       AssertionError: assert SimpleDataObject(a=array([2, 1])) == SimpleDataObject(a=array([1, 2]))
E         Attributes which raised an exception:
E         ['a']
```

Or maybe just handle places where the `__eq__` method is overridden for this issue?

I‘m planning on adding an `__attrs_effective_params__` (https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs/issues/602) but didn’t get around to it yet. :(
